title: This Taiwanese Web Novelist Spent More Than a Decade Trying to Make a Film. What Was He Up Against?
excerpt: Wu Ziyun thought he was ready. He walked onto the set of At Cafe 6 with a resume that was, by then, not so thin — and was lost from the start. "It was like I'd only ever ridden a motorcycle, and suddenly I had to enter a car race."
body:
Wu Ziyun thought he was ready. He walked onto the set of *At Cafe 6* with a resume that was, by then, not so thin — and was lost from the start. "It was like I'd only ever ridden a motorcycle, and suddenly I had to enter a car race."

Right up to the wrap party, Wu still wasn't sure about the film. He was startled to see Hou Hsiao-hsien there, and hurried over to ask for advice. Counting from his directorial debut in 1980, Hou had 36 years behind the camera; Wu was just starting out — until this film, he had been a novelist.

He wanted to ask Hou what a director is supposed to do on set, and how to talk to actors — how, for instance, to convey precisely a flowery instruction like "cry only three-tenths as hard."

"None of that matters," Wu remembers Hou saying. "Director isn't a noun, it's a verb — go direct the performance you want. If it doesn't look like acting at all, that's best." The older director then told a story about shooting in a Japanese bakery: that day, apart from the owner, not one customer realized they had walked onto a film set.

Hou's experience helped Wu work something out.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171210rKtnHTWSbvLXP5zD.jpg-w600)

This was his first time directing. The film was adapted from Wu's own novel *At Cafe 6*, one of the best-known coming-of-age stories in Taiwan. When he wrote the novel, though, his pen name was "Fujii Itsuki" — a name that sounds familiar because he took it from Shunji Iwai's film *Love Letter*. "Fujii Itsuki"'s style does resemble Iwai's; director Wu summed it up vaguely as "very understated stuff."

When a Beijing film and TV company came looking for "Fujii Itsuki," none of that was what drew them. It was something more concrete. "He's Taiwan's best-selling author of romance novels; in Taiwan, only Giddens Ko, the author of *You Are the Apple of My Eye*, can rival him," wrote Zhu Weijie, chairman of Zizai Media and president of Zizai Pictures, in an email reply to QDaily. His company was one of the investors in *At Cafe 6*. The film's lead investor and producer was CTS Entertainment, which had earlier produced and released *So Young*.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171211M8aLVcDFEwR59uKb.jpg-w600)

Like "Fujii Itsuki," Giddens Ko also crossed over from bestselling Taiwanese web novelist to film director — and did it well, which few have. Mainland China's film market keeps putting web novels on screen; in Taiwan, almost no one tried the model again after Pizi Cai's web novel *First Intimate Contact* was filmed in 2000. One reason may be that the adaptation strayed so far from the book that it lost money at the box office.

*You Are the Apple of My Eye* changed what might otherwise have been these web novelists' fate. Some viewers felt the coming-of-age film still ran on most of the genre's worn-out tricks, but more shared the view of Russell Edwards, the critic at *Variety*: "It's one of the more successful, vibrant entries in this kind of coming-of-age story that Taiwan has produced in the past decade." In Taiwan, the film passed NT$100 million in under four days and finished with NT$420 million (about 83.87 million yuan) — a huge take.

The other film brought up again and again during the marketing of *At Cafe 6* was *Our Times*, a Taiwanese coming-of-age picture released the year before, whose numbers were even more startling: in mainland China it grossed more than 300 million yuan, making it the highest-grossing Taiwanese film ever in that market, roughly four times what *You Are the Apple of My Eye* took there.

Wu, though, did not seem to care what those cases meant for *At Cafe 6*, and had no interest in marketing that tied his film to the "blockbusters." At the wrap party, the question gnawing at him was probably close to the one that had gnawed at Giddens Ko: "There's almost no way to win — do it well, and people say you've gotten above yourself, that the novel was just a stepping stone; do it badly, and people say, 'You should have stuck to writing novels.'"

He felt uneasy.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021712119TVnvYaHh8F75KOg.jpg-w600)

In Taiwan, Wu was among the first generation of web novelists. In 1998, the moment he posted his novel *Shall We Not Get Married?* online, it drew a crowd. In the early heyday of BBS forums, web writers updated at speed, competing over who could write the most and the fastest. "There might have been tens of thousands of writers, all fighting over the one or two chances to get published," Wu said.

Huang Shuzhen is now general manager at Cite Publishing, where she oversees the affairs of its many imprints. Back in 1998 she was an editor, and she was the first to spot Wu's novel online. "Even though I was already past thirty, his story stirred up the pure, innocent feelings of my school days," Huang told a media outlet in an earlier interview. After *Shall We Not Get Married?* was formally published in 2000, it climbed the bestseller lists fast, selling about 20,000 copies a month. To date, Fujii Itsuki's books have sold more than 3 million copies.

Yang Ruyu, editor-in-chief of Business Weekly Publications, thinks "Fujii Itsuki" is good at building everyday, lifelike situations and describing feeling in fine detail, and that this is why the books sell. "Fujii Itsuki has a kind of authorial charisma; readers want to follow him and keep reading whatever he writes next."

Most readers who have followed "Fujii Itsuki" over the past few years have noticed that, while he keeps writing, he has been trying to get out from under the "Fujii Itsuki" shadow. On several occasions he has said he would rather be called "Wu Ziyun." The other thing he brings up often is his wish to make a film one day — so often that people began to assume the novelist's real ambition in life was to direct.

When we interviewed him, Wu denied having any such "dream," then described something that amounted to much the same thing: "It's something I have to do in this life... like how some people feel they absolutely have to go bungee jumping, or jump out of a helicopter." Making a film, it seems, was for Wu closer to an extreme sport.

For someone who works in words, turning text into images is genuinely hard. After the idea first came to him in 2004, Wu carried his work around looking for investors, and got nowhere.

Because he couldn't solve the money problem — and maybe because of the excitement and nerves before a "jump" — his efforts in this period took a roundabout path. At first he tried building cinematic elements directly into the writing of *At Cafe 6*, but most readers did not respond to that unusual design. Short on funding, in 2008 Wu shot the short film *A Poem of Summer* (《夏日之诗》). It was a classic tragic romance: a man named A-Jie (played by Roy Chiu) remembers Fenfei, the woman he loved seven years earlier — he once wrote her a poem, and before she died of illness she wrote one back. On this project Wu tried hiring a professional screenwriter to do the adaptation, to spare himself the anguish of "squeezing his own work for juice" — but in the end he took the script back because of the gaps between what the screenwriter wrote and what he meant.

![A Poem of Summer, starring Roy Chiu](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171212Equsvj14wK8rVUmz.jpg-w600)

Before *At Cafe 6* went into production, Wu also directed a music video called *I Am Happy* (《我是幸福的》), about a campus romance. It came out just after *You Are the Apple of My Eye* became a hit.

![Cai Huangru in the music video for I Am Happy](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171212X79sNMKrkY5lVuOP.jpg-w600)

Now Wu felt ready. He walked onto the set of *At Cafe 6* with what was, by then, not such a thin resume — and was lost from the start. "It was like I'd only ever ridden a motorcycle, and suddenly I had to enter a car race."

Shooting ran 89 days, a month longer than planned. Wu later heard that some productions do test shoots first, to learn the location and the crew's habits in advance; his crew shot for real on day one. He also realized for the first time that actors usually have several projects going at once, and that scheduling is a headache.

"One day the executive director and I said the same thing on the same day — 'Why does it feel like we've shot three movies?' Why aren't we done yet, why is this taking so long — my script has been flipped through until it's falling apart."

Nothing went especially wrong, but there was more to smooth out than this Taiwanese novelist had imagined. Turning the novel into a screenplay alone took Wu three full years. And filmmaking is teamwork — faced with a rookie director, everyone seemed to have something to say.

At first Wu nearly gave up on directing. Watching mainland Chinese films over the years, he had decided their taste ran "heavy," which was not a style he was good at. The investors confirmed the worry; they told him plainly: "What you want to make now won't work at all in the mainland market." Coming-of-age films in the mainland tend to be "brutal," and that brutal reality gets reduced to love triangles, affairs, abortions, car crashes.

The mold may have shifted a little after director Frankie Chen found another way in with *Our Times*, but Wu still went through a "pretty grueling" stretch of persuading and being persuaded. "Sometimes we'd end up talking about totally abstract things, using code words for what each of us wanted to do — they called a slap in the face the 'Sword Sect,' so I said I'd use the 'Qi Sect.' Every meeting room turned into a duel — swords coming at me, qi attacks going back — we didn't even feel like eating our lunchboxes."

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171213NUDAhmWPvJuLFEcj.jpg-w600)

![A still from At Cafe 6 (courtesy of CTS Entertainment)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171213lBYa31OFA8cXwjR4.jpg-w600)

What finally tipped the balance may have been the size of the bigger market. In 2015, China's box office came to about 44 billion yuan, while Taiwan's — adding up its ten highest-grossing Chinese-language films — came to roughly NT$1.2 billion (240 million yuan). Wu knew the gap well; he said a whole month of Taiwanese box office probably couldn't beat a single day on the mainland.

That also settled the question of casting a mainland actor as the Taiwanese coming-of-age film's male lead. Zizai Pictures put forward Dong Zijian, a young actor who had been good in films such as *Mountains May Depart*. Wu found it awkward at first: "Having someone from Beijing play a kid from Kaohsiung — there's something logically strange about that."

People kept telling the new director what would be better. The mainland and Taiwanese investors separately brought in Liu Jie and Liao Mingyi as producer and executive director; Liu had also produced *Young Style*, and Liao had worked on *You Are the Apple of My Eye*. It was like having an instructor on a skydive: "I'd throw out my ideas as much as I could, and they'd help me finish the technical part," Wu says.

Wu has since accepted some of these views, and thinks doing it their way really was "better." Before shooting began, for instance, executive director Liao reminded him that *At Cafe 6* would be marketed as a commercial film, so he would have to give up some of his personal style. "If I'm going to cut beef, I should buy a beef knife to begin with," Wu explained.

Then the problem came back to the film itself. After the shoot, Wu went to Hong Kong, where the editor Zhang Jiahui cut the picture. Wu's daily job was to carry a small notebook and write down what the edit had to watch for and which shots needed fixing — "uncomfortable every single day." As he understands it, almost every director goes through a painful stretch like this once shooting ends, tearing things down and building them again.

At the wrap party on May 15 last year, Wu felt lost. He told himself to stop thinking about making films — he probably never wanted to take the challenge a second time.

![A still from At Cafe 6 (courtesy of CTS Entertainment)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171213borHUpk0dh9qeR6L.jpg-w600)

But now Wu seems to have changed his mind. When we interviewed him this past May, he said: "If you ask me right now whether I want to shoot another one, I find myself thinking, 'Do I?' ... It's not that I'd absolutely refuse..."

The novelist has also formed some first observations about the film industry. He has noticed that the relationship between web writers and the movie business is speeding up. It wasn't like that before: Wu wanted to make a film in 2004, and it took him ten years to find investors.

Wu has always insisted he is not a "writer": "I don't think I'll ever be qualified to be called a writer in this lifetime. Writing novels makes you a scribe, the way driving makes you a driver. I didn't come up through some traditional literary competition — my results are just what the times happened to produce, I was simply lucky." But clearly, if all of it is to be put down to "luck," web writers' luck today runs further than that.

![Wu Ziyun, director of At Cafe 6 (photo by Chen Liya)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171214BjIA3NpRM8tFH9PL.jpg-w600)

**Below, Q = QDaily, W = Wu Ziyun**

**Q: In turning this novel into a film, what was the most dangerous part?**

W: With *At Cafe 6*, the investors would try to tell you that what you want to make now won't work at all in the mainland market, and I did worry about that, because deep down I understood — that bigger market is right there, and one day there wipes out a month here. But later I relaxed about it, because I'm not famous over there either (laughs), so it made no difference. I decided to take care of the Taiwan box office first.

**Q: You first published your novels on BBS forums. Do you know the equivalent forum sites on the mainland? Do you know mainland web-literature writers? What do you make of them?**

W: Mostly, yes. People like Guo Jingming, Han Han, Tianxia Bachang (Zhang Muye), Tang Jia San Shao — I roughly know what genres they each write.

That said, I don't read much fantasy myself. Beyond that, mainland web literature is fairly different from ours in language and usage. And mainland web literature seems to have a habit of writing a lot — a book isn't satisfied until it runs to several million characters. Without a lot of patience, I really don't think you can finish it.

**Q: A lot of people think Taiwan's film market is small. What do you think?**

W: As long as something counts as a "domestic film" — a Taiwanese film — it's small. At most two million people in Taiwan will buy a ticket, and the box office comes to just over NT$700 million; the mainland might take in 700 million yuan in a single day.

I don't think this is a question of market size. It's whether, once a work comes out, Taiwan can keep its filmmakers fed — keep them from losing so much that they can't make the next one. If *At Cafe 6* does badly, will there be a chance to make another? Maybe, maybe not. But I can go back to writing novels; I still have a rice bowl. What about someone who does nothing but make films?

A healthy market needs many genres to raise its audience. Director Hou (Hou Hsiao-hsien) and director Tsai (Tsai Ming-liang) have their own audiences; there's also our sort, the kind that makes people laugh out loud, or something like *David Loman*, made for mom to watch. Films of every kind competing together in a free market — that's healthy. Right now we're in the transition into a healthy competitive environment.

**Q: *At Cafe 6* was a novel from 2007, and it took eight years to reach the screen. With a popular novel — unless it's a serial, or the characters pull a strong following — how do you handle that time gap before the film?**

W: If you mean whether the original readers will come back... well, I hope they come back (laughs).

**Q: Your latest novel, *The Shadow Social Worker*, has a different subject, and its readership has probably shifted too. How do you handle that?**

W: I'm actually not sure whether the readership has changed, because *The Shadow Social Worker* didn't sell well. A lot of people said, "This isn't Wu Ziyun." By the standards of the publishing market its sales were fine; when I say it didn't sell well, I mean compared with my other books. People just can't accept it: one moment I'm writing about falling in love, and then I've gone off to "kill people." But I can't fall in love forever — and anyway, I wanted to kill someone.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021712140JZSBLqtkfjzxeYw.jpg-w600)

**Q: What's the most recent book you've read and the most recent film you've seen? What did you think?**

W: For a film, *White Lies, Black Lies* was one of them. The most recent thing I've read is a video-game magazine (laughs) — for the strategy guides. Any woman who's dated me has had it rough; they think I'm childish, as if I'll die without video games. Look at me, I turn forty this year, and at forty I'm still playing video games.

Cover image courtesy of CTS Entertainment.
